## Three Open Questions

::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-teal}
1
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
**Evaluation:** How do we measure whether a forecast is good
for the *decision* it informs?
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-purple}
2
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
**Training:** Can we design a DFL method that is both
decision-aware *and* probabilistically well-calibrated?
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-coral}
3
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
**Benchmarking:** Which DFL methods actually work, and when?
What guidance can we give practitioners?
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
This is the thesis overview dressed up as open questions. Each maps to a chapter.
:::

## The opportunities created by existing literature

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-teal-light}
1
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
Models were rarely compared to competitors or reasonable baselines, making the benefit of any model impossible to determine.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-teal}
2
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
Existing literature nearly unanimously used error-based metrics to compare models, making the effects of using such models to guide policy decisions unclear.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-teal-dark}
3
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
Code rarely shared, data nearly never shared.
:::
:::
:::


## The Task

<iframe src="figures/choropleth.pdf" style="width: 100%; height: 440px; border: none;" title="MA opioid overdose deaths choropleth"></iframe>

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.4;"}
**Prediction Target**

$y$ = number of deaths in a census tract next year

::: {.fragment}
**Input Variables**

$x$ = Location, Time, Demographics, Last year's overdose counts, Social Vulnerability Index
:::
:::


## Prior State-of-the-Art

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em; margin-bottom: auto;"}

| Year | Base Model | + Social Determinants of Health |
|:----:|:----------:|:-------------------------------:|
| 2016 | 2.35       | 2.40                            |
| 2017 | 2.04       | 1.94                            |
| 2018 | 2.47       | 2.44                            |
| 2019 | 2.19       | 2.18                            |

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.42em; color: var(--muted); border-top: 1px solid var(--separator); padding-top: 0.5em; margin-top: 1.5em;"}
Bauer C, Zhang K, Li W, Bernson D, Dammann O, LaRochelle MR, Stopka TJ. Small Area Forecasting of Opioid-Related Mortality: Bayesian Spatiotemporal Dynamic Modeling Approach. *JMIR Public Health Surveill* 2023;9:e41450.
:::

## Takeaways

::: {.fragment .card style="border-left: 4px solid var(--teal-light);"}
Simple models can be strong — these should be included in future work
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-teal}
If these models will be used for decision-making, we should use decision-based metrics like %BPR
:::

::: {.fragment .card style="border-left: 4px solid var(--teal-dark);"}
Our code and *data* are available at <https://github.com/tufts-ml/opioid-overdose-models>
:::


# Training {background-color="#1a0a2a"}

::::: {.columns style="margin-top: 1.5em;"}

:::: {.column width="75%"}
**Decision-aware Training of Spatiotemporal Forecasting Models to Select a Top-K Subset of Sites for Intervention**

<br>

Kyle Heuton, Frederick Muench, Shikhar Shrestha, Thomas J. Stopka, Michael C. Hughes

[*Proceedings of the Forty-Second International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)*, 2025]{.muted}
::::

:::: {.column width="25%" style="display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: flex-start; padding-top: 0.3em;"}

## The opportunities created by existing literature {background-image="figures/crane.svg" background-size="22%" background-position="left bottom" background-opacity="0.25"}

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-purple-light}
1
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
Decision-aware metrics do not have informative gradients — it is unclear how to optimize for them.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-purple}
2
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
Given a probabilistic model for events, it isn't clear how to best rank locations.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.contribution-item}
::: {.contribution-num .accent-purple-dark}
3
:::
::: {.contribution-body}
Existing decision-aware methods sacrifice model likelihood.
:::
:::
:::

:::::: {.ranking-math-slide style="margin-top: 0.4em; font-size: 0.86em;"}

:::: {.math-scroll-inner style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 63% 37%; gap: 0 1.2em;"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1;"}
A natural framework: minimize the expected loss

$$\mathbf{s}^* = \underset{\mathbf{s}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y} \sim p_{\theta}} \!\left[ L( \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{y} ) \right]$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3 style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; align-self: start; background: var(--bg-card); border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; padding: 1em;"}
[Why not just the mean?]{.accent-yellow style="font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.05em;"}

$$\bar{\mathbf{s}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\mathbf{y}]$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2;"}
Define the **BPR loss** ($\mathbf{s}$ = score vector):

$$L^{\text{BPR}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{y}) = -\frac{\mathbf{y} \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{s}, K)}{\mathbf{y} \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{y}, K)}$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 3;"}
Sub in $L^{\text{BPR}}$:

$$\mathbf{s}^* = \underset{\mathbf{s}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y} \sim p_{\theta}} \!\left[ -\frac{\mathbf{y} \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{s}, K)}{\mathbf{y} \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{y}, K)} \right]$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=5 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 4;"}
Bound denominator:

$$\mathbf{s}^* = \underset{\mathbf{s}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y} \sim p_{\theta}} \!\left[ - \underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{y} \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{s}, K)}{K \cdot U}}_{\leq \;\text{BPR}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{y})} \right]$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=5 style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 4; align-self: center; background: var(--bg-card); border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; padding: 1em;"}
[Extreme Upper Bound]{.accent-coral style="font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.05em;"}

$U \geq y_i$ for any $i$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=6 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 5;"}
Linearity of expectation:

$$\mathbf{s}^* = \underset{\mathbf{s}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}} - \underbrace{\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}}[\mathbf{y}] \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{s}, K)}{K \cdot U}}_{\leq \;\text{BPR}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{y})}$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=7 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 6;"}
**$\mathbf{s} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\mathbf{y}]$ is a valid solution.**
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=7 style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 6; align-self: center; background: var(--bg-card); border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; padding: 1em;"}
$\mathbf{s}$ can be any $\mathbf{s}$ such that

$\operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{s}, K) = \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\mathbf{y}], K)$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=8 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 7; border-top: 1px solid var(--separator); padding-top: 0.8em; margin-top: 0.4em;"}
Tighter bound:

$$\mathbf{s}^* = \underset{\mathbf{s}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}} - \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y} \sim p_{\theta}}\!\left[\frac{\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{y}}\right] \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{s}, K)}_{\leq \;\text{BPR}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{y})}$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=8 style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 7; align-self: center; background: var(--bg-card); border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; padding: 1em;"}
[Tighter Bound]{.accent-teal style="font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.05em;"}

$\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{y} \geq \mathbf{y} \cdot \operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{y}, K)$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=9 style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 8;"}
**The ratio estimator:**

$$\mathbf{s}^* = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y} \sim p_{\theta}}\!\left[\frac{\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{y}}\right] \approx \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} \frac{\mathbf{y}^{(m)}}{\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{y}^{(m)}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=9 style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 8; align-self: center; background: var(--bg-card); border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; padding: 1em;"}
$\mathbf{s}$ can be any $\mathbf{s}$ such that

$\operatorname{TopKMask}(\mathbf{s}, K) = \operatorname{TopKMask}\!\left(\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}\!\left[\tfrac{\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{y}}\right], K\right)$
:::

::::

```{=html}
<script>
window.addEventListener('load', function () {
  if (typeof Reveal === 'undefined') return;
  var container = document.querySelector('.ranking-math-slide');
  if (!container) return;

  // Tune: scroll fires when bottom of new content exceeds THRESH of container height;
  // PADDING keeps that much content visible above the bottom edge after scrolling.
  var THRESH  = 0.6;
  var PADDING = 260;

  function inContainer(frags) {
    return frags.filter(function (f) { return container.contains(f); });
  }

  function fragBounds(frags) {
    var cr = container.getBoundingClientRect();
    var minTop = Infinity, maxBot = -Infinity;
    frags.forEach(function (f) {
      var r = f.getBoundingClientRect();
      var t = r.top    - cr.top + container.scrollTop;
      var b = r.bottom - cr.top + container.scrollTop;
      if (t < minTop) minTop = t;
      if (b > maxBot) maxBot = b;
    });
    return { top: minTop, bottom: maxBot };
  }

  Reveal.on('fragmentshown', function (e) {
    var frags = inContainer(e.fragments || [e.fragment]);
    if (!frags.length) return;
    var bounds  = fragBounds(frags);
    var visible = container.clientHeight;
    if (bounds.bottom > container.scrollTop + visible * THRESH) {
      var target = bounds.bottom - visible + PADDING;
      if (target > container.scrollTop)
        container.scrollTo({ top: target, behavior: 'smooth' });
    }
  });

  Reveal.on('fragmenthidden', function (e) {
    var frags = inContainer(e.fragments || [e.fragment]);
    if (!frags.length) return;
    var bounds = fragBounds(frags);
    var target = Math.max(0, bounds.bottom - container.clientHeight + PADDING);
    if (target < container.scrollTop)
      container.scrollTo({ top: target, behavior: 'smooth' });
  });

  Reveal.on('slidechanged', function () {
    setTimeout(function () {
      var c = document.querySelector('.present .ranking-math-slide');
      if (c) c.scrollTop = 0;
    }, 0);
  });
});
</script>
```

## Training takeaways

::: {.fragment .card .card-purple-light}
Differentiable perturbed optimizers allow us to train models that make better decisions
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-purple}
When we care about ranking, the ratio estimator is superior to taking the mean of a distribution
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-purple-dark}
The Decision-Aware Maximum Likelihood objective can deliver high-quality decisions and high-likelihood models
:::

## Benchmarking takeaways

::: {.fragment .card .card-coral}
Existing decision-aware benchmarks don't use decision-aware tasks
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-coral-dark}
Future efforts should focus on the loss landscape induced by a given method
:::


# Conclusion and Future Work {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

## Conclusion

::: {.fragment .card .card-teal}
**Best Possible Reach** — a decision-oriented evaluation metric shows that simpler models can be just as strong, and that error-based metrics miss what matters for policy
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-purple}
**DAML** — by jointly optimizing decision quality and likelihood, we can navigate the training frontier and avoid sacrificing calibration for performance
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-coral}
**Benchmarking** — existing evaluations don't use decision-aware tasks; the loss landscape induced by a method is a better lens for understanding when DFL helps
:::


## Future Directions

::: {.fragment .card .card-coral}
Better benchmarks and deeper understanding of the loss landscape of decision-aware methods
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-purple}
More intelligent training methods for decision-aware learning — which samples matter the most?
:::

::: {.fragment .card .card-teal}
Decision-aware model training and inference
:::
